note: Rav Ḥisda sent Rav Naḥman a question: the Sages fixed payments for kneeing, kicking and punching someone, so what is owed for a blow with a hoe? Rav Naḥman replied: Ḥisda, Ḥisda, are you collecting fines in Babylonia? Tell me what actually happened. Rav Ḥisda explained: two men shared a cistern, each drawing water on alternate days. One drew on the other's day, ignored him when told it was not his turn, and was struck with the handle of a hoe. Rav Naḥman answered that he deserved a hundred blows, since even those who forbid taking the law into one's own hands allow it to prevent a loss.
why: The Gemara uses this case to open a dispute: Rav Yehuda says a person may not take the law into his own hands, Rav Naḥman says he may, and all agree he may when a loss is imminent.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sent Rav Naḥman a question about payment for a blow with a hoe, then described the case.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Answered that the man struck with the hoe deserved it.

terms.meaning: A fixed penalty set by the Sages, as opposed to paying for actual loss. Babylonian courts could not impose such fines.

terms.term: taking justice into one's own hands
terms.meaning: Enforcing one's rights oneself rather than going to court.

note: A man cut down another man's date palm, and the two came before the Exilarch. The Exilarch said he had seen the spot himself: three palms grew there in a cluster, worth a hundred dinars together, so the man must pay thirty-three and a third. The man objected that the Exilarch judged by Persian law and took the case to Rav Naḥman, who ruled that the damage is appraised as part of an area sixty times larger.
why: The Gemara has just explained a baraita as teaching that damage to a field is valued as part of an area sixty times larger. Rav Naḥman applies that rule here; Rava then asks whether it applies when a person does the damage himself, as here, and not only his animal.

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who first judged the case and set payment at a third of the palms' value.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judged the case again and ruled by the one-in-sixty appraisal.

terms.meaning: Valuing the damaged part as one-sixtieth of a larger plot, which yields a lower payment than valuing it alone.
The law of the ruling Persian state, as opposed to Torah law.
